3. Direct-Drive (Continuous Drive) Friction Welding

One component is held in a rotating chuck driven continuously by a motor; the other is held stationary. The two are brought together under axial force and rubbed until the interface reaches forging condition. Rotation is then stopped by braking, and forge force is applied.

Characteristics:

• Rotational speed is held constant through the heating phase.

• Heating time and upset are the controlled variables, and the cycle can be controlled by time, by upset distance, or by a combination.

• The braking stage matters. How fast rotation stops relative to when the forge force is applied determines whether forging happens into hot, plastic mate

1. Procedure Qualification and Welder Qualification Prove Different Things

These two are constantly confused, and the distinction is simple once stated.

Procedure qualification (Chapter 31) proves that a set of welding conditions produces a joint with the required properties. Its tests are property tests: tensile, impact, hardness, macro. It is welded by a competent welder precisely so that welder skill is not the variable under examination.

Welder qualification proves that a specific person can produce a sound weld using a given process in a given configuration. Its tests are soundness tests: bend tests, radiography, fracture tests. It does not test tensile strength or toughness, because those are properties of the procedure, not of the person.

5. Carbon Migration and Why the Joint Degrades in Service

Carbon migration is the mechanism that makes an apparently sound dissimilar joint fail years later.

At elevated temperature, carbon in the ferritic or low-alloy steel diffuses toward the chromium-rich material because chromium's affinity for carbon lowers the chemical potential of carbon there. Two damaged bands result, on either side of the interface:

• A decarburized, soft band in the low-alloy steel, weakened and prone to creep deformation.

• A carburized, hard, brittle band in the high-chromium material, prone to cracking.

Hot cracking. Umbrella term for cracking at high temperature during or shortly after solidification. Includes solidification cracking and liquation cracking. (Ch. 23, 24, 26)

Hydrogen-assisted cracking (HAC). Also cold cracking or delayed cracking. Requires four conditions together: diffusible hydrogen, a susceptible microstructure, tensile stress, and a temperature range near ambient. 12. The Inspection Problem

Beam welds present a genuine inspection difficulty that arc welds do not, and it is worth stating explicitly because inspection plans carried over from arc welding fail here:

The weld is very narrow. A fusion zone a fraction of a millimetre wide is difficult to interrogate — ultrasonic beams must be positioned precisely, and a small misalignment misses the weld entirely. The same narrowness that makes the process attractive makes it hard to inspect.

Welding is governed by three large standards systems — ISO (with EN as its European adoption), AWS, and ASME — that developed independently, use different vocabulary for the same physics, and are not interchangeable. Card 1 — Filler balls up and will not flow into the joint

12. In-Service Welding on Operating Pipelines

A specific and technically demanding case: welding onto a pipeline that continues to carry product. It is done to install branch connections and repair sleeves without shutting down the line, and it presents two competing risks that must be balanced against each other:

Risk 1 — Burn-through. The pipe wall is thinned by the welding heat while internal pressure acts on it. If the remaining wall cannot contain the pressure, it fails. This risk decreases with lower heat input.

Risk 2 — Hydrogen cracking. The flowing contents remove heat from the joint rapidly — a substantial quench — producing a hard heat-affected zone. Combined with hydrogen, this risk increases with lower heat input, because lower heat input means faster cooling.

3. The Cost Model

The cost of a welded joint decomposes cleanly. Every term below is measurable locally.

Weld metal required — cross-sectional area of the joint (from the preparation geometry) multiplied by length, multiplied by density. This is set by the *designer*, not by the welding department.

Arc time — weld metal required, divided by deposition rate, divided by deposition efficiency.

Total labour time — arc time divided by the operating factor (arc time as a fraction of the welder's paid time). This single division is where most of the cost lives.

Labour cost — total labour time multiplied by the fully burdened labour rate.

Pipe qualification adds diameter as a variable, because welding a small-bore pipe is a substantially different manipulation problem from welding a large-diameter one — the torch angle changes continuously around a small circumference and access is restricted.

• Penetration is shallow relative to steel at the same current. The weld goes where the arc puts it, and no further.

• Lack of sidewall fusion is the characteristic defect, because the pool will not run up the groove face on its own.

Resistance spot welding (RSW) is a resistance-welding process that produces a weld at the faying (contacting) surfaces between overlapping parts, using heat obtained from the resistance to the flow of welding current through the parts, combined with the application of mechanical force through the electrodes [S9]. It belongs to the pressure-welding family: unlike arc or laser welding, no filler metal is added and no arc is struck. The joint forms entirely from localized resistive heating under clamping force, which is why the process is sometimes described to newcomers as "welding by squeezing and cooking," a simplification that is directionally correct even though it skips the electrical detail that actually governs weld quality.

Magnetic pulse welding discharges a large stored electrical charge through a coil placed around or beside a workpiece. The resulting intense, rapidly changing magnetic field induces opposing currents in the workpiece, and the interaction between the field and those induced currents produces a repulsive force that accelerates the workpiece across a small gap onto a mating part. • Fume from the detonation products.

QUESTION: What safety requirements must be met for explosion welding operations?

Licensed explosives handling, storage and use is a legal requirement, with licensed personnel. Separation distances and exclusion zones for blast, noise and fragments must be established. The flux rule that matters most: an aggressive flux gives better wetting and leaves a residue that will corrode the joint if not removed. On a plumbing joint the residue can be washed off. 4. Range of Approval: Pipe Diameter

Pipe qualification adds diameter as a variable, because welding a small-bore pipe is a substantially different manipulation problem from welding a large-diameter one — the torch angle changes continuously around a small circumference and access is restricted.

The cost of a welded joint decomposes cleanly. Every term below is measurable locally.

Weld metal required — cross-sectional area of the joint (from the preparation geometry) multiplied by length, multiplied by density. This is set by the *designer*, not by the welding department.

Engineering practice targets the center of the lobe to minimize production variation effects such as tip wear, force fluctuation, minor material variation, and line-voltage sag. Preheat acts before and during welding, to control the cooling rate and to keep the joint out of the hydrogen cracking window while hydrogen escapes.

Interpass temperature acts during welding, and is controlled in both directions — as a minimum for the same reasons as preheat, and as a maximum to prevent cumulative heat from degrading the microstructure.

Post-weld heat treatment acts after welding is complete, principally to relieve residual stress and to temper hard microstructures, and it can do neither of the first two jobs.

4. The Upset: Forging Out the Molten Metal

The upset is the quality-determining stage. Its controlled variables:

• Upset distance — how far the parts advance during forging. Too little leaves contaminated interface material in the joint; too much wastes material and can produce excessive flash and grain flow distortion.

1. Imperfection, Defect and the Distinction That Matters

The two words are not interchangeable in standards language, and the distinction carries real consequences.

An imperfection is any deviation from the ideal weld. Every weld ever made contains imperfections. A weld with no imperfections does not exist, and a report that finds none has either not looked properly or is describing a weld inspected by a method incapable of finding what is there.

A defect is an imperfection that exceeds the acceptance criteria applicable to that weld. It is a judgement made by comparing an observed imperfection against a specified limit.

Traceability is the ability to connect a completed weld to the conditions under which it was made. The elements normally required:

• Which parent material heat or cast the joint was made in.

• What heat treatment the joint received, and the record of that cycle.

• What inspection was performed, by whom, and with what result.

This is the central engineering issue with both processes, and it is inherent rather than a fault to be tuned out.

What happens. The very high heat input and the very large molten volume give an extremely slow cooling rate. Three consequences follow from putting the flux inside the wire rather than outside a stick electrode:

Deposition rate is high. Out-of-position capability is excellent. The slag freezes quickly and physically supports the molten pool against gravity. 2. Why the Tubular Construction Changes the Process

Three consequences follow from putting the flux inside the wire rather than outside a stick electrode:

Deposition rate is high. Current is carried by the thin metal sheath rather than by the full cross-section, so current density in the conducting metal is very high, and burn-off rate rises accordingly. Out-of-position capability is excellent. The slag freezes quickly and physically supports the molten pool against gravity. 1. Two Applications of One Idea

This chapter covers two families that share a single principle: a welding process used to deposit metal rather than to join two parts.

Additive manufacturing builds a component from nothing, layer by layer, from wire or powder.

Surfacing — cladding, hardfacing, buttering and weld repair — deposits a layer onto an existing component to give it a surface property it does not have, or to restore material it has lost.

The processes are the same ones from Volume 3 and Chapter 52. 9. Matching, Undermatching and Overmatching

Filler strength relative to the parent metal is a deliberate design decision with three possible answers.

Matching — filler strength approximately equal to parent strength — is the default for most structural work and is what prequalified procedures assume.

Undermatching — filler weaker than the parent — is used deliberately in three situations: where the weld is not the critical load path and a lower-strength, more ductile deposit reduces cracking risk; where a lower-strength consumable has lower hydrogen sensitivity on a high-strength parent; and in fillet welds on high-strength steel, where a full-strength fillet is often not required by the design and an undermatched consumable reduces both cost and cracking risk. In structural steelwork, the quality level is not chosen by the fabricator — it is derived from the execution class assigned to the structure, which is determined at design stage from consequence of failure, service category (static or fatigue-loaded) and production category.

12. Parameters and Their Control

The welding parameters are those of the process chapters; automation changes how they are managed:

• Parameters are stored in the programme, so the same values are used every time — the consistency benefit.

• Parameters can vary along the joint under programme control: ramping current around a corner, changing at a thickness transition, adapting to a sensed gap.

• Start and stop sequences — pre-flow, hot start, crater fill, burnback, post-flow — are programmed rather than manual, and they are where a large share of automated weld defects occur.

• Every weld's actual parameters can be recorded, giving a complete process record (Section 16).

• Parameter drift is invisible without monitoring, because nobody is watching.

1. Process Overview: The Two High-Frequency Variants

High-frequency welding produces the longitudinal seam in welded tube and pipe, continuously, at line speeds that make it the dominant process for commodity tubular product. Flat strip is roll-formed progressively into a tube shape with the two strip edges approaching each other, the edges are heated to forging temperature by high-frequency current, and squeeze rolls forge them together — expelling the molten and oxidized material as an internal and external bead.

1. Imperfection, Defect and the Distinction That Matters

The two words are not interchangeable in standards language, and the distinction carries real consequences.

An imperfection is any deviation from the ideal weld. Every weld ever made contains imperfections. A weld with no imperfections does not exist, and a report that finds none has either not looked properly or is describing a weld inspected by a method incapable of finding what is there.

A defect is an imperfection that exceeds the acceptance criteria applicable to that weld. It is a judgement made by comparing an observed imperfection against a specified limit.

Group 4 contains the processes that make a joint without melting the parent metal. Pipe qualification adds diameter as a variable, because welding a small-bore pipe is a substantially different manipulation problem from welding a large-diameter one — the torch angle changes continuously around a small circumference and access is restricted.

15. Troubleshooting Cards

Card 1 — Weld looks perfect, sectioning shows no joint

Symptom: an acceptable-looking bead with the joint unfused beneath it.

Category: missed joint.

Likely causes: beam offset from the joint line; on EBW, residual magnetism deflecting the beam; gap exceeding bridging capability; part positioning or fixture variation; seam tracking not functioning or not enabled.

9. Titanium, and Joints That Need a Transition Piece

Titanium forms brittle intermetallics with iron, nickel and copper. Direct fusion welding of titanium to steel is not a viable structural route.

Where such a joint is required — chemical plant, marine, aerospace — the standard solutions are an explosion-welded transition joint (Section 10) or an interlayer of a metal that is compatible with both, such as vanadium or niobium, deposited in a controlled sequence. Both are specialist operations.

Other pairs requiring similar treatment: copper to steel (interlayer or transition joint for structural applications), and any pairing where a phase diagram shows intermetallic compounds across the composition range of interest. 5. Where the Hydrogen Comes From and How It Is Controlled

Sources, in rough order of how often they are the actual cause:

• Moisture in consumable coverings or fluxes. Basic covered electrodes and submerged arc fluxes are hygroscopic. An electrode that meets a low-hydrogen classification when it leaves the factory does not meet it after a day in humid air.

• Moisture, oil, grease, rust and paint on the joint surfaces. Hydrocarbons and hydrated oxides dissociate in the arc.

• Moisture in the shielding gas or in gas lines, particularly after a line has been opened or a new cylinder connected.

• Water leaks onto the join

QUESTION: What are the common sources of hydrogen in welding processes?

Common sources of hydrogen include moisture in consumable coverings or fluxes, moisture/oil/grease/rust/paint on joint surfaces, moisture in shielding gas or gas lines, water leaks from cooling circuits, and the consumable's own chemistry. [3]

Welders and engineers who arrive at aluminium from a steel background consistently underestimate it, and the reason is that aluminium violates the sensory cues that steel practice is built on.

6. Fluxes and Atmospheres

Wetting requires a clean, oxide-free surface at brazing temperature, and there are two routes to it:

Flux — a chemical applied to the joint that dissolves existing oxide and prevents reformation during heating. Fluxes are formulated for specific temperature ranges and filler systems, and using a flux outside its active temperature range is equivalent to using no flux at all: it will be exhausted before the filler melts, or not yet active when it does.

- Higher current is not automatically better. Because heat scales with I², a modest increase can push a marginal weld from "acceptable, small nugget" straight past "good" into "expulsion and electrode damage," with very little current margin in between on a thin, high-conductivity stack.

5. Upset (Resistance Butt) Welding: The Simpler Relative

Upset welding heats the joint without flashing. The parts are held in firm contact under force from the start, and current flows continuously through the contact interface, heating it by bulk resistance until the material reaches forging temperature. The parts are then upset together.

Differences from flash welding:

• No flashing stage, so no expulsion of material during heating and no self-cleaning action — the faying surfaces must therefore be clean and squarely cut before welding.

• Heating is slower and more uniform through the section.

• No sparks, so it is cleaner and quieter in operation.

• Limited to smaller cross-sections in p

Current is fed through sliding contacts — shoes or wheels — bearing on the strip surface on each side of the open seam, upstream of the weld point. Current flows from one contact, along the edge toward the weld point, across the closing gap at the apex, back along the other edge, and out through the second contact.

Characteristics:

• High electrical efficiency, because current is delivered directly into the strip.

• Suits larger diameters and heavier walls, where induction coupling becomes inefficient.

• The contacts are consumables that wear

Aluminium alloys crack during solidification by the general mechanism of Chapter 22 — but with a distinctive and highly useful relationship to composition.

For the major alloying elements, crack sensitivity plotted against alloy content produces a curve with a peak at low-to-intermediate alloy content and lower sensitivity both below and above it. The process depends entirely on two electromagnetic phenomena, and understanding them explains why it works at all.

4. Keyhole Mode

Above the power density threshold, metal vaporizes and the vapour pressure displaces the melt, opening a narrow cavity — the keyhole — that extends into or through the material. 14. Why Misnaming a Process Invalidates Qualification

In every qualification system covered in Chapter 31, the welding process is an essential variable — meaning a change to it requires requalification rather than merely a revised procedure document. This is not bureaucratic conservatism. Three concrete mechanisms sit behind it:

Different processes deposit different metal. A 111 electrode and a 136 wire nominally matched to the same base metal will not produce identical weld-metal chemistry, because the flux systems, deoxidizer packages and dilution behaviour differ. Mechanical properties follow chemistry, and a qualification test proves mechanical properties.

Requires four conditions together: diffusible hydrogen, a susceptible microstructure, tensile stress, and a temperature range near ambient. 12. The Inspection Problem

Beam welds present a genuine inspection difficulty that arc welds do not, and it is worth stating explicitly because inspection plans carried over from arc welding fail here:

The weld is very narrow. A fusion zone a fraction of a millimetre wide is difficult to interrogate — ultrasonic beams must be positioned precisely, and a small misalignment misses the weld entirely. The same narrowness that makes the process attractive makes it hard to inspect.

Planar defects lie along the joint plane. The missed joint and lack of fusion are exactly the defects radiography detects worst (Chapter 35, Section 1), and they are among the most likely in this process.

1. Procedure Qualification and Welder Qualification Prove Different Things

These two are constantly confused, and the distinction is simple once stated.

Procedure qualification (Chapter 31) proves that a set of welding conditions produces a joint with the required properties. Its tests are property tests: tensile, impact, hardness, macro. It is welded by a competent welder precisely so that welder skill is not the variable under examination.

Welder qualification proves that a specific person can produce a sound weld using a given process in a given configuration. Its tests are soundness tests: bend tests, radiography, fracture tests. It does not test tensile strength or toughness, because those are properties of the procedure, not of the person.

3. The Threshold Deformation

This is the process's defining characteristic and the fact that governs every design decision around it.

Below a threshold amount of deformation, no bond forms at all. Not a weak bond — no bond. The surface expansion has been insufficient to fracture the oxide film and extrude virgin metal through it.

Above the threshold, bond strength rises rapidly with further deformation, as the bonded fraction increases.

The threshold is material-specific and is expressed as a percentage reduction in thickness or area. It is typically substantial — for aluminium it is a large fraction of the original thickness, and for harder metals it is higher still. This has direct consequences:

8. Braze Welding: The Exception to Capillary Action

Braze welding deposits a brazing filler into a groove or fillet, exactly like a weld bead, without relying on capillary action and without melting the parent metal.

Why it exists: it gives a joint that looks and functions like a weld, at a much lower temperature than fusion welding — which matters where the parent metal cannot tolerate welding temperatures.

Its main application is cast iron (Chapter 26, Section 10): braze welding avoids the high-carbon melting, the hard heat-affected zone and the cracking that fusion welding of cast iron risks. It is a standard cast iron repair method and frequently the best one.

Three consequences follow from putting the flux inside the wire rather than outside a stick electrode:

Deposition rate is high. Out-of-position capability is excellent. The slag freezes quickly and physically supports the molten pool against gravity. Pipe qualification adds diameter as a variable, because welding a small-bore pipe is a substantially different manipulation problem from welding a large-diameter one — the torch angle changes continuously around a small circumference and access is restricted.

8. Eddy Current and Other Surface Methods

Eddy current testing induces circulating currents in a conductive material with a coil, and detects the perturbation those currents suffer at a discontinuity. It works on any electrically conductive material — including non-ferromagnetic ones, unlike magnetic particle testing — detects surface and near-surface defects, requires no couplant, and can work through thin non-conductive coatings, which is a substantial practical advantage on painted structures.

Its limitations are shallow penetration, sensitivity to material property and geometry variation (which produces indications unrelated to defects), and interpretation difficulty.

7. Root Drop-Out and Underfill

Root drop-out: molten metal falling out of the root of a full-penetration weld because surface tension cannot support it. Causes: excessive power for the thickness, travel too slow, and no root support.

Underfill: the weld surface below the parent surface, because material was lost — expelled as spatter or vapour — and no filler was added to replace it. This is inherent to autogenous beam welding: the process removes material and adds none.

18. Safety Specifics

Laser safety differs from arc welding safety in kind, not merely in degree:

• The beam is invisible at the near-infrared and far-infrared wavelengths used for welding. There is no visual warning, and the eye's blink reflex offers no protection.

• Eye damage occurs at very low power compared with the welding beam's power, and near-infrared wavelengths reach the retina — a focused near-infrared beam can cause permanent retinal damage from a stray reflection.

• Reflections are a primary hazard. A specular reflection from a shiny workpiece, a fixture or a tool carries substantial power in an unpredictable direction. Thi

3. Nickel Alloys: Hot Cracking and the Contamination That Causes It

Nickel alloys are strongly susceptible to solidification and liquation cracking, and they are unusually sensitive to low-melting-point contaminants. Elements that form low-melting compounds with nickel — sulphur, phosphorus, lead, zinc, tin, bismuth — produce intergranular liquid films at grain boundaries that tear under contraction stress.

The severity of this cannot be overstated and it makes cleanliness a first-order engineering control rather than good housekeeping. Realistic contamination sources in an ordinary workshop:

A servo welding gun positions and closes its electrodes using an electric servo motor and drive rather than a pneumatic cylinder acting against a fixed regulated pressure. The generic functional chain, regardless of manufacturer, is the same: a servo controller/drive commands a motor, the motor drives a mechanical transmission (typically a ballscrew or an equivalent linear-motion mechanism), the transmission moves the gun arm/electrode holder, and the electrode makes contact with the part. e half of the AC cycle, ions bombard the workpiece surface and break up the oxide film — the cathodic cleaning effect. On the electrode-negative half, heat goes into the work and provides penetration.

Modern AC power sources allow the balance between the two halves to be adjusted, and this is a direct, continuous trade:

A servo welding gun positions and closes its electrodes using an electric servo motor and drive rather than a pneumatic cylinder acting against a fixed regulated pressure. The generic functional chain, regardless of manufacturer, is the same: a servo controller/drive commands a motor, the motor drives a mechanical transmission (typically a ballscrew or an equivalent linear-motion mechanism), the transmission moves the gun arm/electrode holder, and the electrode makes contact with the part. Cold pressure welding joins metals at room temperature, with no applied heat at all, purely by plastic deformation under pressure. 10. Reheat Cracking in Creep-Resistant Steels

Also called stress-relief cracking. It occurs during post-weld heat treatment or during high-temperature service, not during welding.

Mechanism. In creep-resistant steels containing strong carbide formers — chromium, molybdenum, vanadium, niobium — the coarse-grained heat-affected zone is left after welding with those elements in solution. On reheating to stress-relief temperature, fine carbides precipitate inside the grains, strengthening the grain interiors relative to the grain boundaries. Residual stress then relaxes preferentially by sliding at the weakened boundaries, and intergranular cracks form in the coarse-grained heat-affected zone.

Susceptible materials: Cr-Mo and Cr-Mo-V creep-resistant steels, some stainless grades stabilized with niobium, and some nickel

6. Knurl Patterns and Tooling

The sonotrode and anvil faces are patterned — knurled, serrated or textured — and this is functional rather than cosmetic:

• The pattern grips the workpiece, so that the sonotrode's motion is transmitted into the upper part rather than sliding across its surface. Without grip, the vibration scrubs the tool against the part instead of scrubbing the two parts against each other.

• The anvil pattern grips the lower part so it does not move with the upper one.

• Pattern geometry affects marking on the workpiece surface — deeper, coarser patterns grip better and mark more.

The two lessons.

The first is the one in Section 11: control part accuracy before automating, not after. The manual process had been concealing a fit-up problem, and automation revealed it in the most expensive possible way.

The second is about the business case itself. The case was not dishonest; it was built by people who did not know what the manual welders were compensating for, because that compensation had never been measured. Aluminium alloys crack during solidification by the general mechanism of Chapter 22 — but with a distinctive and highly useful relationship to composition.

For the major alloying elements, crack sensitivity plotted against alloy content produces a curve with a peak at low-to-intermediate alloy content and lower sensitivity both below and above it. Pure aluminium has a narrow freezing range and does not crack; a small alloying addition widens the freezing range and creates a large, weak mushy zone with just enough liquid to form a continuous film but not enough to backfill tears as they form — the worst case; higher alloy content produces enough eutectic liquid to flow into and heal incipient tears, so sensitivity falls again.

3. Keyhole Instability: The Mechanism Behind Most Beam Defects

The keyhole is a vapour cavity held open by vaporization pressure against surface tension and the hydrostatic head of surrounding molten metal. That balance is dynamic — the cavity fluctuates in depth and shape continuously, at high frequency.

Four defect types trace directly to those fluctuations:

| Fluctuation behaviour | Resulting defect |
| --- | --- |
| Momentary collapse trapping vapour at the root | Root porosity |
| Periodic deep excursions of the cavity tip | Spiking, often with pores at the spike tips |
| Melt flow instability around a fast-moving keyhole | Humping |
| Cavity breaking through with insufficient surface tension to hold the root | Root drop-out |

This is the central engineering issue with both processes, and it is inherent rather than a fault to be tuned out.

What happens. The very high heat input and the very large molten volume give an extremely slow cooling rate. 9. Matching, Undermatching and Overmatching

Filler strength relative to the parent metal is a deliberate design decision with three possible answers.

Matching — filler strength approximately equal to parent strength — is the default for most structural work and is what prequalified procedures assume.

Undermatching — filler weaker than the parent — is used deliberately in three situations: where the weld is not the critical load path and a lower-strength, more ductile deposit reduces cracking risk; where a lower-strength consumable has lower hydrogen sensitivity on a high-strength parent; and in fillet welds on high-strength steel, where a full-strength fillet is often not required by the design and an undermatched consumable reduces both cost and cracking risk. FCAW — and self-shielded FCAW in particular — generates substantially more fume than gas-shielded solid wire processes for comparable deposition. 10. The Fit-Up Problem

This is the process's defining practical limitation, and it decides more laser welding projects than any metallurgical consideration.

The mechanism. A focused beam may be a few tenths of a millimetre across. A butt joint with a gap wider than the beam presents nothing for the beam to strike — it passes through, melting the edges inadequately or not at all. There is no filler being added and no wide arc cone to bridge the gap, so the process cannot compensate for a gap the way any arc process can.

Card 1 — Worm-hole porosity appearing in cold, damp conditions

Symptom: elongated cavities along the weld, worse on the first welds of the day.

Category: consumable condition.

Likely causes: moisture absorbed into the wire core from humid storage or an exposed spool; condensation on the joint surface; no warm-through applied on cold material.

Steps: check wire storage and whether the spool was left on the machine overnight; check whether partly used spools are resealed; apply a warm-through to remove surface moisture from cold material; confirm the joint is dry before welding.

This is the process's defining practical limitation, and it decides more laser welding projects than any metallurgical consideration.

The mechanism. A focused beam may be a few tenths of a millimetre across. Filler strength relative to the parent metal is a deliberate design decision with three possible answers.

Matching — filler strength approximately equal to parent strength — is the default for most structural work and is what prequalified procedures assume.

This is the central technical difficulty of WAAM and the source of most of its defects.

Three defining characteristics distinguish it from welding:

1. The parent metal is not melted. It is heated, and it must be wetted by the filler, but it stays solid throughout.

Symptom: most parts good, some with lack of fusion or misplaced welds; no pattern in time.

Category: part or fixture variation.

PAW covers an unusually wide current range, and it behaves as three distinct processes across it:

Microplasma, at very low currents — fractions of an ampere up to a few amperes. The constricted arc remains stable and directional at currents where a free GTAW arc would be unstable and wander. Melt-in mode, at intermediate currents. The pool is melted from the surface downward, as in GTAW, with better penetration and standoff tolerance. Used for general welding, root passes and thin sheet.

• Ozone generation is significant on aluminium and on high-current argon-shielded work, from UV acting on atmospheric oxygen (Chapter 37, Section 6).

Hydrogen is highly soluble in molten aluminium and almost insoluble in solid aluminium. The total electrical resistance in a spot-welding circuit is the sum of several resistances in series: the bulk resistance of each sheet, the contact resistance at each sheet-to-sheet (faying) interface, and the contact resistance at each electrode-to-sheet interface. For structural steels, the electrical and thermal conductivity of the workpiece is far lower than that of the copper-alloy electrodes, so under Joule heating (Q = I²Rt) the heat is generated disproportionately at the sheet interfaces rather than in the electrodes or the bulk of the sheet [S13]. This is the entire reason spot welding of steel works efficiently with copper tooling: copper carries the current with low loss, and the workpiece itself becomes the resistive heating element at the one location — the faying interface — where heat is actually wanted.

Resistance spot welding (RSW) is a resistance-welding process that produces a weld at the faying (contacting) surfaces between overlapping parts, using heat obtained from the resistance to the flow of welding current through the parts, combined with the application of mechanical force through the electrodes [S9]. It belongs to the pressure-welding family: unlike arc or laser welding, no filler metal is added and no arc is struck. The joint forms entirely from localized resistive heating under clamping force, which is why the process is sometimes described to newcomers as "welding by squeezing and cooking," a simplification that is directionally correct even though it skips the electrical detail that actually governs weld quality.

7. The Tube Mill as a System

High-frequency welding never exists as a standalone operation; it is one station in a continuous mill, and its quality depends on everything upstream:

Uncoiler and strip preparation → accumulator (allowing continuous running through coil changes) → forming section (progressively rolling flat strip into a tubular shape) → fin pass (setting the final edge geometry and vee) → weld station (HF power, contacts or coil, impeder, squeeze rolls) → bead removal (external, and internal where required) → cooling → sizing section → cut-off.

The sonotrode and anvil faces are patterned — knurled, serrated or textured — and this is functional rather than cosmetic:

• The pattern grips the workpiece, so that the sonotrode's motion is transmitted into the upper part rather than sliding across its surface. Without grip, the vibration scrubs the tool against the part instead of scrubbing the two parts against each other.

• The anvil pattern grips the lower part so it does not move with the upper one.

• Pattern geometry affects marking on the workpiece surface — deeper, coarser patterns grip better and mark more.

The total electrical resistance in a spot-welding circuit is the sum of several resistances in series: the bulk resistance of each sheet, the contact resistance at each sheet-to-sheet (faying) interface, and the contact resistance at each electrode-to-sheet interface. For structural steels, the electrical and thermal conductivity of the workpiece is far lower than that of the copper-alloy electrodes, so under Joule heating (Q = I²Rt) the heat is generated disproportionately at the sheet interfaces rather than in the electrodes or the bulk of the sheet [S13]. This is the entire reason spot welding of steel works efficiently with copper tooling: copper carries the current with low loss, and the workpiece itself becomes the resistive heating element at the one location — the faying interface — where heat is actually wanted.

Deposition rate is high. A Welding Procedure Specification (WPS) is a controlled engineering document that specifies a qualified — or otherwise formally approved — set of welding conditions, together with the scope of parts, materials and equipment to which those conditions apply [S7]. It is a quality-system document before it is anything else: it exists to record what has been proven to work, under what conditions, and it carries the approval, revision and traceability metadata needed to answer "is this the currently valid procedure for this joint" at any later point. That last requirement — resolvability at any later point — is why a WPS cannot be treated as a one-time engineering artifact that is written once and then referred to loosely; it has to survive audits, root-cause investigations and customer reviews years after it was first approved.

3. The Intermetallic Layer: The Joint's Real Interface

This is the most important concept in soldering and the one that distinguishes a superficial understanding from a working one.

A soldered joint is not solder stuck to metal. At the interface, the solder reacts with the base metal to form a thin layer of intermetallic compound — typically copper-tin compounds on a copper substrate. That layer is the actual bond. Without it there is no metallurgical joint, only mechanical adhesion.

Three consequences govern joint reliability:

A thin intermetallic layer is necessary and good. It demonstrates that a metallurgical reaction occurred. A joint with no intermetallic layer has not properly wetted and will fail.

2. Skin Effect and Proximity Effect: Why the Current Goes Where It Is Wanted

The process depends entirely on two electromagnetic phenomena, and understanding them explains why it works at all.

Skin effect. Alternating current does not distribute evenly through a conductor's cross-section; it concentrates toward the surface, and the higher the frequency, the shallower the layer it occupies. At the frequencies used in this process — high radio frequencies, far above mains frequency — the current flows in an extremely thin surface layer.

Proximity effect. When two conductors carrying current in opposite directions run close together, the current in each concentrates on the faces nearest the other.

3. Range of Approval: Thickness

The test coupon thickness determines the production thickness range the welder may weld. Under ISO 9606-1 the ranges are banded by test thickness, with the general pattern that a test on material of thickness *t* qualifies from a stated minimum up to 2t [S2].

For example, a test on a 12 mm plate butt weld gives a range of approval from 3 mm to 24 mm [S2].

Testing thicker qualifies more. A shop that tests everyone on thin material to save consumables and time will find its welders unqualified for the heavier work in the same production mix.

5. Upset (Resistance Butt) Welding: The Simpler Relative

Upset welding heats the joint without flashing. The parts are held in firm contact under force from the start, and current flows continuously through the contact interface, heating it by bulk resistance until the material reaches forging temperature. The parts are then upset together.

Differences from flash welding:

• No flashing stage, so no expulsion of material during heating and no self-cleaning action — the faying surfaces must therefore be clean and squarely cut before welding.

• Heating is slower and more uniform through the section.

• No sparks, so it is cleaner and quieter in operation.

• Limited to smaller cross-sections in p

Hydrogen is highly soluble in molten aluminium and almost insoluble in solid aluminium. Nickel alloys are strongly susceptible to solidification and liquation cracking, and they are unusually sensitive to low-melting-point contaminants. Elements that form low-melting compounds with nickel — sulphur, phosphorus, lead, zinc, tin, bismuth — produce intergranular liquid films at grain boundaries that tear under contraction stress.

Cold pressure welding works by defeating that film mechanically:

1. Surface preparation removes the existing oxide and leaves a hard, brittle, freshly formed thin oxide over clean metal (Section 4).

2. Deformation. The parts are pressed together and forced to deform substantially. As the metal beneath the surface flows plastically, the surface area increases dramatically.

3. Film fracture. The oxide film is hard and brittle relative to the metal beneath it. It cannot stretch with the expanding surface, so it fractures into islands.

4. Virgin metal extrusion. Clean metal from beneath is extruded through the gaps between the oxide fragments.

5. Bonding. Where virgin metal from one part meets virgin metal from the other under pressure, a metallic bond forms instantly.

Through-hole with wave soldering: component leads pass through plated holes; the board passes over a molten solder wave; capillary action fills the barrel. Joint quality is judged partly by barrel fill — the extent to which solder rose through the hole.

A two-sheet stack has one faying interface: essentially all of the resistive heat this chapter's formulas are describing is generated at that single interface, bounded on either side by the two sheets' bulk resistance and by the electrode contact resistance at the two outer faces. A three-sheet stack is a materially different electrical and thermal problem, not simply "the same thing with more metal": current passes through two faying interfaces in series plus the bulk of the center sheet, and Chapter 2 is explicit that the heat generated — and the resulting nugget — is not necessarily symmetric between those two interfaces, particularly when the two outer sheets differ from one another in thickness, grade or coating.

4. Range of Approval: Pipe Diameter

Pipe qualification adds diameter as a variable, because welding a small-bore pipe is a substantially different manipulation problem from welding a large-diameter one — the torch angle changes continuously around a small circumference and access is restricted.

Under ISO 9606-1 the pattern is that small-diameter tests qualify a limited band around the tested diameter, while tests above a certain diameter qualify without an upper limit [S2]. A two-sheet stack has one faying interface: essentially all of the resistive heat this chapter's formulas are describing is generated at that single interface, bounded on either side by the two sheets' bulk resistance and by the electrode contact resistance at the two outer faces. The total electrical resistance in a spot-welding circuit is the sum of several resistances in series: the bulk resistance of each sheet, the contact resistance at each sheet-to-sheet (faying) interface, and the contact resistance at each electrode-to-sheet interface. For structural steels, the electrical and thermal conductivity of the workpiece is far lower than that of the copper-alloy electrodes, so under Joule heating (Q = I²Rt) the heat is generated disproportionately at the sheet interfaces rather than in the electrodes or the bulk of the sheet [S13]. This is the entire reason spot welding of steel works efficiently with copper tooling: copper carries the current with low loss, and the workpiece itself becomes the resistive heating element at the one location — the faying interface — where heat is actually wanted.

1. Process Overview and the 450 °C Boundary

Soldering joins components with a filler metal that melts below 450 °C, drawn into the joint by capillary action, without melting the parent materials. It is mechanically identical to brazing (Chapter 66) and distinguished from it only by that temperature boundary — which sits in the ISO nomenclature's group 9 alongside brazing and braze welding [S1].

The boundary is conventional but not arbitrary: it separates two families of filler alloys, two ranges of achievable strength, and two largely separate industrial disciplines.

12. Parameters and Their Control

The welding parameters are those of the process chapters; automation changes how they are managed:

• Parameters are stored in the programme, so the same values are used every time — the consistency benefit.

• Parameters can vary along the joint under programme control: ramping current around a corner, changing at a thickness transition, adapting to a sensed gap.

• Start and stop sequences — pre-flow, hot start, crater fill, burnback, post-flow — are programmed rather than manual, and they are where a large share of automated weld defects occur.

• Every weld's actual parameters can be recorded, giving a complete process record (Section 16).

• Parameter drift is invisible without monitoring, because nobody is watching.

Copper pipework is the classic application: capillary fittings with a controlled clearance, heated with a torch, with solder drawn into the joint by capillary action.

Practical points:

• The joint must be clean — abrasive cleaning of both pipe end and fitting socket, then flux applied to both.

• Heat the fitting, not the solder. Solder touched to the hot joint should melt on contact and be drawn in; melting it with the flame is the same error as in brazing (Chapter 66, Section 10).

• A complete ring of solder at the fitting mouth is the evidence that capillary action filled the joint.

• Do not disturb the joint while it solidifies.

• Remove flux residues — acid fluxes will corrode the joint and the pipe.

9. Lamellar Tearing

A distinct mechanism that occurs in the parent plate, not the weld, and only under a specific loading geometry.

Mechanism. Rolled plate contains non-metallic inclusions — principally manganese sulphides and silicates — that are flattened into planes parallel to the rolled surface. The plate is therefore weaker in the through-thickness direction than in the rolling direction. When a weld imposes contraction stress in the through-thickness direction, these flattened inclusions decohere and link, producing a stepped, terrace-like crack running parallel to the plate surface below the weld.

1. Process Overview: The Two High-Frequency Variants

High-frequency welding produces the longitudinal seam in welded tube and pipe, continuously, at line speeds that make it the dominant process for commodity tubular product. 10. Pulsed GTAW

Pulsing alternates a peak current that establishes penetration with a lower background current that lets the pool partially solidify. Its advantages:

• Lower average heat input for the same penetration, reducing distortion on thin material.

• Better pool control out of position, since the pool partially freezes between pulses.

• Consistent penetration on varying thickness or fit-up, because the peak does the fusing.

• A characteristic stacked-coin bead appearance

QUESTION: What is the sequence of events during the explosion welding process?

1. Setup. The flyer plate is positioned above the base plate at a controlled standoff distance, either parallel or at a small initial angle. An explosive layer of controlled thickness and detonation velocity is placed on the flyer's upper surface, usually over a protective buffer layer. 2. Detonation. The charge is initiated at one point and the detonation front travels across the plate at a defined velocity. 3. Progressive acceleration. 3. The Intermetallic Layer: The Joint's Real Interface

This is the most important concept in soldering and the one that distinguishes a superficial understanding from a working one.

A soldered joint is not solder stuck to metal. At the interface, the solder reacts with the base metal to form a thin layer of intermetallic compound — typically copper-tin compounds on a copper substrate. That layer is the actual bond. A thin intermetallic layer is necessary and good. It demonstrates that a metallurgical reaction occurred. A joint with no intermetallic layer has not properly wetted and will fail.

5. Upset (Resistance Butt) Welding: The Simpler Relative

Upset welding heats the joint without flashing. The parts are held in firm contact under force from the start, and current flows continuously through the contact interface, heating it by bulk resistance until the material reaches forging temperature. The parts are then upset together.

Differences from flash welding:

• No flashing stage, so no expulsion of material during heating and no self-cleaning action — the faying surfaces must therefore be clean and squarely cut before welding.

• Heating is slower and more uniform through the section.

• No sparks, so it is cleaner and quieter in operation.

9. Matching, Undermatching and Overmatching

Filler strength relative to the parent metal is a deliberate design decision with three possible answers.

Matching — filler strength approximately equal to parent strength — is the default for most structural work and is what prequalified procedures assume.

8. The Missed Joint and Lack of Fusion

The most dangerous beam welding defect, because the weld can look entirely acceptable.

How it happens:

• The beam is offset from the joint line — by a teaching error, seam tracking failure, part positioning variation, or fixture wear.

• On EBW specifically: residual magnetism deflects the beam (Chapter 53, Section 8), which is a cause with no equivalent anywhere else in this reference set.

• The gap exceeds the beam's ability to bridge it, so the beam passes through without melting both faces adequately (Chapter 52, Section 10).

• Part-to-part fit-up variation takes some parts outside the tolerance while others stay inside — producing intermittent failures on nominally identical parts.

10. Reheat Cracking in Creep-Resistant Steels

Also called stress-relief cracking. It occurs during post-weld heat treatment or during high-temperature service, not during welding.

Mechanism. In creep-resistant steels containing strong carbide formers — chromium, molybdenum, vanadium, niobium — the coarse-grained heat-affected zone is left after welding with those elements in solution. On reheating to stress-relief temperature, fine carbides precipitate inside the grains, strengthening the grain interiors relative to the grain boundaries. Residual stress then relaxes preferentially by sliding at the weakened boundaries, and intergranular cracks form in the coarse-grained heat-affected zone.

4. Range of Approval: Pipe Diameter

Pipe qualification adds diameter as a variable, because welding a small-bore pipe is a substantially different manipulation problem from welding a large-diameter one — the torch angle changes continuously around a small circumference and access is restricted.

Under ISO 9606-1 the pattern is that small-diameter tests qualify a limited band around the tested diameter, while tests above a certain diameter qualify without an upper limit [S2]. Larger test pieces therefore qualify more broadly, and the same logic as thickness applies: testing on the smallest available pipe is the cheapest test and the narrowest qualification.

This is a real and initially baffling phenomenon that GTAW users on stainless steel meet sooner or later, and it deserves explicit treatment because it is routinely misdiagnosed as an equipment fault.

The observation: two plates of the same specification, from different heats, welded autogenously with identical parameters, produce visibly different penetration — one deep and narrow, the other wide and shallow.

The mechanism is the Marangoni effect (Chapter 22, Section 5). Surface tension varies with temperature, and the sign of that variation depends on trace elements — sulphur and oxygen in particular, at concentrations of tens of parts per million. With sufficient trace sulphur, the surface flow carries hot metal inward and down, giving a deep narrow pool. Without it, the flow runs outward, giving a wide shallow pool.

8. Eddy Current and Other Surface Methods

Eddy current testing induces circulating currents in a conductive material with a coil, and detects the perturbation those currents suffer at a discontinuity. It works on any electrically conductive material — including non-ferromagnetic ones, unlike magnetic particle testing — detects surface and near-surface defects, requires no couplant, and can work through thin non-conductive coatings, which is a substantial practical advantage on painted structures.

Its limitations are shallow penetration, sensitivity to material property and geometry variation (which produces indications unrelated to defects), and interpretation difficulty.

3. The Cost Model

The cost of a welded joint decomposes cleanly. Every term below is measurable locally.

Weld metal required — cross-sectional area of the joint (from the preparation geometry) multiplied by length, multiplied by density. This is set by the *designer*, not by the welding department.

Arc time — weld metal required, divided by deposition rate, divided by deposition efficiency.

Total labour time — arc time divided by the operating factor (arc time as a fraction of the welder's paid time). This single division is where most of the cost lives.

Labour cost — total labour time multiplied by the fully burdened labour rate.

3. The Cost Model

The cost of a welded joint decomposes cleanly. Every term below is measurable locally.

Weld metal required — cross-sectional area of the joint (from the preparation geometry) multiplied by length, multiplied by density. This is set by the *designer*, not by the welding department.

9. Electronics Soldering Processes

Through-hole with wave soldering: component leads pass through plated holes; the board passes over a molten solder wave; capillary action fills the barrel. Joint quality is judged partly by barrel fill — the extent to which solder rose through the hole.

Surface mount with reflow: solder paste (solder powder plus flux in a carrier) is printed through a stencil onto the pads, components are placed onto the wet paste, and the assembly is heated through a controlled profile. The paste collapses, flux activates, solder melts, and surface tension self-centres the components onto their pads — a genuinely useful self-correcting effect.

8. Flow Rate, Nozzle and the Turbulence Trap

More gas is not better shielding, and this is one of the most persistent misconceptions on the shop floor.

Shielding depends on laminar flow — a smooth column of gas displacing air. Above a certain flow rate for a given nozzle, the flow becomes turbulent, and turbulent flow entrains the surrounding air into the shielding column. The result is that increasing flow past that point makes porosity worse, not better. A welder responding to porosity by turning the flowmeter up is a common and self-defeating sequence.

16. Safety Specifics

• High-frequency electromagnetic fields at significant power. Exposure limits, shielding of the weld station, and the specific hazard to implanted medical devices apply (Chapter 37, Section 10). This is a more substantial consideration here than in arc welding.

• High voltages in the HF power supply.

• Molten metal expulsion at the weld point, continuously along a running line.

• Moving strip and rotating rolls at speed — the dominant mechanical hazard, with entanglement and crushing points throughout the mill.

• Hot product downstream of the weld station.

• Noise from the mill and from the HF supply.

8. Flow Rate, Nozzle and the Turbulence Trap

More gas is not better shielding, and this is one of the most persistent misconceptions on the shop floor.

Shielding depends on laminar flow — a smooth column of gas displacing air. Above a certain flow rate for a given nozzle, the flow becomes turbulent, and turbulent flow entrains the surrounding air into the shielding column. The result is that increasing flow past that point makes porosity worse, not better. A welder responding to porosity by turning the flowmeter up is a common and self-defeating sequence.

1. Procedure Qualification and Welder Qualification Prove Different Things

These two are constantly confused, and the distinction is simple once stated.

Procedure qualification (Chapter 31) proves that a set of welding conditions produces a joint with the required properties. Its tests are property tests: tensile, impact, hardness, macro. It is welded by a competent welder precisely so that welder skill is not the variable under examination.

Welder qualification proves that a specific person can produce a sound weld using a given process in a given configuration. Its tests are soundness tests: bend tests, radiography, fracture tests. It does not test tensile strength or toughness, because those are properties of the procedure, not of the person.

Resistance spot welding (RSW) is a resistance-welding process that produces a weld at the faying (contacting) surfaces between overlapping parts, using heat obtained from the resistance to the flow of welding current through the parts, combined with the application of mechanical force through the electrodes [S9]. It belongs to the pressure-welding family: unlike arc or laser welding, no filler metal is added and no arc is struck. 6. Fluxes and Atmospheres

Wetting requires a clean, oxide-free surface at brazing temperature, and there are two routes to it:

Flux — a chemical applied to the joint that dissolves existing oxide and prevents reformation during heating. Fluxes are formulated for specific temperature ranges and filler systems, and using a flux outside its active temperature range is equivalent to using no flux at all: it will be exhausted before the filler melts, or not yet active when it does.

Flux residues are corrosive and must be removed after brazing — usually by hot water washing, sometimes chemically. Residues left in a joint cause corrosion in service, and this is a common cause of delayed failure.

Controlled atmosphere or vacuum — furnace brazing under a reducing atmospher

Controlled atmosphere or vacuum — furnace brazing under a reducing atmosphere (hydrogen or dissociated ammonia), an inert atmosphere, or vacuum removes the need for flux entirely. [1]

1. Procedure Qualification and Welder Qualification Prove Different Things

These two are constantly confused, and the distinction is simple once stated.

Procedure qualification (Chapter 31) proves that a set of welding conditions produces a joint with the required properties. Its tests are property tests: tensile, impact, hardness, macro. It is welded by a competent welder precisely so that welder skill is not the variable under examination.

Welder qualification proves that a specific person can produce a sound weld using a given process in a given configuration. Its tests are soundness tests: bend tests, radiography, fracture tests. It does not test tensile strength or toughness, because those are properties of the procedure, not of the person.

17. Worked Example: Worm-Hole Porosity on a Structure Welded in Winter

Situation. A steel erection contractor using self-shielded FCAW on site finds elongated worm-hole porosity in radiographs of welds made during a cold, wet week. Welds from the previous month were clean. Same wire specification, same welders, same machines.

Step 1 — Read the defect type as evidence. Worm-hole porosity — elongated cavities rather than round pores — indicates a sustained gas source escaping through metal that is solidifying around it, rather than a momentary shielding disturbance. That points at moisture or contamination present continuously, not at an intermittent shielding failure (Chapter 36, Section 4).

Symptom: molten filler sits on the surface as a bead rather than wetting and flowing.

• Adhesive: low equipment cost, high surface preparation cost, and cure time is a production constraint requiring fixturing or handling strength before the assembly can move.

Preheat acts before and during welding, to control the cooling rate and to keep the joint out of the hydrogen cracking window while hydrogen escapes.

Interpass temperature acts during welding, and is controlled in both directions — as a minimum for the same reasons as preheat, and as a maximum to prevent cumulative heat from degrading the microstructure.

1. Imperfection, Defect and the Distinction That Matters

The two words are not interchangeable in standards language, and the distinction carries real consequences.

An imperfection is any deviation from the ideal weld. Every weld ever made contains imperfections. A weld with no imperfections does not exist, and a report that finds none has either not looked properly or is describing a weld inspected by a method incapable of finding what is there.

A defect is an imperfection that exceeds the acceptance criteria applicable to that weld. It is a judgement made by comparing an observed imperfection against a specified limit.

. Why Beam Welds Fail Differently

Beam welds — laser (Chapter 52) and electron beam (Chapter 53) — share a defect population that arc welding does not produce, and lack several that arc welding does.

What they do not suffer from: slag inclusions (no flux), tungsten inclusions (no electrode), electrode-related defects, and the shielding failures that dominate arc welding porosity. Spatter is present but is a minor issue compared with consumable-electrode arc processes.

What they do suffer from, and arc welding does not:

• Keyhole dynamics defects — porosity, spiking, humping — arising from the instability of a vapour cavity held open by pressure against surface tension.

• The missed joint — a beam narrower than the joint tolerance can miss the joint entirely, producing a weld that is visually acceptable and structurally absent.

8. Fire and Explosion

Welding and cutting are the classic hot work hazards, and hot work fires characteristically injure people who were not welding and start in places nobody was watching.

The mechanisms:

• Sparks and spatter travel — a substantial horizontal distance on the flat, and much further when falling from height. They find combustibles through floor openings, wall penetrations, conveyor gaps and cable routes.

• Conduction through the material. The far side of a wall or bulkhead can ignite insulation or stored material, without any spark travelling at all. This is the mechanism behind many serious hot work fires and it defeats a fire watch that only watches the visible side.

3. Manual Pipe Welding Practice

Established practice, worth stating because orbital welding automates it:

Root pass options:

• GTAW root (141) — the highest-quality option, giving precise pool control and a smooth internal profile; requires purging; the standard for stainless, alloy and high-quality carbon steel work.

• Cellulosic SMAW root (E6010/E6011) — deep penetrating, fast-freezing, forgiving of an open root, welded downhill at speed; the pipeline standard for carbon steel, and explicitly not low-hydrogen (Chapter 38, Section 4).

• Consumable insert — a preplaced ring fused into the root, giving a consistent root profile (Section 9).

Fill and cap: SMAW with low-hydrogen electrodes, FCAW, or GMAW — chosen on deposition rate and code permission.

Situation. A manufacturer welds a medium-volume steel assembly by robotic GMAW. A laser cell is proposed. This is a real and initially baffling phenomenon that GTAW users on stainless steel meet sooner or later, and it deserves explicit treatment because it is routinely misdiagnosed as an equipment fault.

The observation: two plates of the same specification, from different heats, welded autogenously with identical parameters, produce visibly different penetration — one deep and narrow, the other wide and shallow.

The mechanism is the Marangoni effect (Chapter 22, Section 5). Surface tension varies with temperature, and the sign of that variation depends on trace elements — sulphur and oxygen in particular, at concentrations of tens of parts per million. With sufficient trace sulphur, the surface flow carries hot metal inward and down, giving a deep narrow pool. Without it, the flow runs outward, giving a wide shallow pool.

6. Knurl Patterns and Tooling

The sonotrode and anvil faces are patterned — knurled, serrated or textured — and this is functional rather than cosmetic:

• The pattern grips the workpiece, so that the sonotrode's motion is transmitted into the upper part rather than sliding across its surface. Without grip, the vibration scrubs the tool against the part instead of scrubbing the two parts against each other.

• The anvil pattern grips the lower part so it does not move with the upper one.

• Pattern geometry affects marking on the workpiece surface — deeper, coarser patterns grip better and mark more.

The most dangerous beam welding defect, because the weld can look entirely acceptable.

The most dangerous beam welding defect, because the weld can look entirely acceptable.

• The gap exceeds the beam's ability to bridge it, so the beam passes through without melting both faces adequately (Chapter 52, Section 10).

• Part-to-part fit-up variation takes some parts outside the tolerance while others stay inside — producing intermittent failures on nominally identical parts.

8. Joint Design and Fit-Up

EBW's fit-up requirements are the tightest of any process in this reference set, for the same reason as laser welding (Chapter 52, Section 10) but more severely, because the beam is narrower and no filler is normally added.

Requirements:

• Square butt joints with essentially zero gap are the standard configuration. The beam melts the two faces together; there is nothing to bridge a gap with.

• Machined joint faces are normal, not exceptional. Sheared or flame-cut edges are generally inadequate.

• Alignment tolerance is a fraction of the beam diameter.

• Self-locating joint designs — spigots, interlocking features, shrink fits — are used deliberately so that the joint's own geometry guarantees alignment.

Automation changes the quality strategy fundamentally:

What improves: parameter consistency; complete process data on every weld; repeatable travel speed and torch position; controlled heat input; and elimination of welder-to-welder variation.

• UV output is high — the constricted arc is intense — with the same radiation controls as GTAW plus attention to reflection from the bright plasma column.

• High-frequency starting, where used, generates electromagnetic interference.

Symptom: most parts good, some with lack of fusion or misplaced welds; no pattern in time.

The upset is the quality-determining stage. Its controlled variables:

• Upset distance — how far the parts advance during forging. Too little leaves contaminated interface material in the joint; too much wastes material and can produce excessive flash and grain flow distortion.

• Upset force — must be sufficient to extrude the molten material and forge the parent metal. Insufficient force is the most common root cause of flat fractures.

• Upset speed — must be fast enough that the interface does not cool and oxidize before the forge closes it. A sluggish upset allows oxidation between the end of flashing and the closing of the joint.

• Upset current — current continuing into the upset stage keeps the material hot and plastic through the forging.

15. Safety Specifics

• The pilot arc is live whenever it is running, even between welds, and it is a genuine burn hazard on a manual torch.

• UV output is high — the constricted arc is intense — with the same radiation controls as GTAW plus attention to reflection from the bright plasma column.

• Noise from the plasma jet at higher gas flows can be significant, more so in cutting configurations (Chapter 64).

• Ozone generation from UV acting on atmospheric oxygen, as GTAW.

• High-frequency starting, where used, generates electromagnetic interference.

• Water-cooled torches carry a coolant leak hazard onto a live electrical assembly; leak checking is part of routine maintenance.

• Thoriated tungsten grinding dust applies as in GTAW (Chapter 41, Section 18).

vidence of a sound weld. Metallographic examination of an explosion weld looks first for a regular, continuous wave pattern.

• They increase the bonded area and mechanically interlock the two metals.

• Wave amplitude and wavelength vary with the parameters, and their character indicates where in the weldability window the weld was made.

• A flat interface is not necessarily unbonded, but it indicates conditions at the edge of the window.

• Excessive melting at the wave vortices — visible as pockets of solidified material, often intermetallic on dissimilar joints — indicates too much energy, and those pockets are brittle and are a defect.

12. The Inspection Problem

Beam welds present a genuine inspection difficulty that arc welds do not, and it is worth stating explicitly because inspection plans carried over from arc welding fail here:

• Penetration is shallow relative to steel at the same current. The weld goes where the arc puts it, and no further.

15. Safety Specifics

• The pilot arc is live whenever it is running, even between welds, and it is a genuine burn hazard on a manual torch.

• UV output is high — the constricted arc is intense — with the same radiation controls as GTAW plus attention to reflection from the bright plasma column.

• Noise from the plasma jet at higher gas flows can be significant, more so in cutting configurations (Chapter 64).

• Ozone generation from UV acting on atmospheric oxygen, as GTAW.

• High-frequency starting, where used, generates electromagnetic interference.

• Water-cooled torches carry a coolant leak hazard onto a live electrical assembly; leak checking is part of routine maintenance.

• Thoriated tungsten grinding dust applies as in GTAW (Chapter 41, Section 18).
